doc:
How to draw the rider's own position — the mark, and the circle of uncertainty around it (`docs/proposals/06 §6b`). Two rules, both exact equality. Neither invents a value it was not given: a missing heading is a DOT and not a north-pointing dart, and a missing accuracy is no circle rather than a guessed one. That is ADR-008 applied to position instead of time, and it has teeth here because a rider orienting themselves at a kerb acts on the answer immediately.

**Non-finite readings are spelled `"NaN"` and `"Infinity"` as STRINGS**, because JSON has neither. A suite must decode them to its own language's non-finite values before calling — the rows that use them exist to pin that a non-finite reading is treated as *no reading*, so a port that passed the string straight through would be testing string handling and reporting a pass.

cases.name: a-compass-heading-is-the-dart
cases.why: The best case, and the question a rider standing still is actually asking — which way am I facing. Only a true compass answers it.

cases.name: the-compass-wins-over-course-when-both-are-present
cases.why: The precedence, and the row that matters most. A rider who granted compass permission and then stopped walking still has a compass and no course — but a rider WALKING has both, and taking the course there would swing their dart to their direction of travel every time they glanced at the map. Facing beats moving.

cases.name: course-over-ground-is-the-fallback
cases.why: No compass — no permission, or a desktop browser that has none. Course answers a different question and answers it well enough while the rider is moving, which is the only time it answers at all. The value is 44.2 rather than a round number on purpose, and it earned its keep immediately: an implementation that normalises unconditionally returns 44.19999999999999, because `((deg % 360) + 360) % 360` is two operations that cannot be exact in binary. A bearing already in range must pass through untouched.

cases.name: a-stationary-rider-with-no-compass-gets-a-dot
cases.why: The COMMON case on a stationary phone, not an edge case: course over ground is null exactly when a rider is standing at a bus stop. This is the row that makes the dot the default rather than the failure.

cases.name: absent-fields-are-the-same-as-null
cases.why: A platform that omits a key rather than nulling it — Android and iOS adapters differ here, and a JSON round-trip turns one into the other. Both mean the same thing and must produce the same mark.

cases.name: due-north-is-a-heading-not-a-missing-one
cases.why: The falsy trap, and the one an `if (heading)` gets wrong: 0 is NORTH, a perfectly good answer, and a port testing truthiness turns every north-facing rider into a dot. The mirror of the row above; the two only make sense together.

cases.name: a-negative-bearing-is-normalised-not-rejected
cases.why: Adapters correct for platform differences by subtracting — device-orientation alpha runs the other way on some Android builds — and can land just below zero. Normalising means an adapter's arithmetic cannot produce a mark pointing at nothing, and the bug would otherwise be invisible on whichever platform did not have it.

cases.name: a-bearing-past-a-full-turn-wraps
cases.why: The other end of the same normalisation. 450 degrees is 90, and a port that clamped rather than wrapping would point a quarter-turn wrong instead of obviously wrong.

cases.name: a-non-finite-heading-is-no-heading-at-all
cases.why: A sensor that has not settled, or a division nobody guarded. A non-finite reading IS an absence and is treated as one — a dart at an undefined angle renders pointing north on some engines and vanishes on others, and both are worse than a dot. A port checking only for null passes every row above and fails this one.

cases.name: a-non-finite-compass-still-falls-through-to-the-course
cases.why: The same guard, and it must not swallow the fallback: an unusable compass reading leaves the course still worth reading. A port that returned a dot as soon as the compass was non-null would throw away a heading it had.

locationMark.doc:
Which mark to draw for the rider's own position: a dart where a heading is known, a dot where it is not. Exact equality; `bearing` is degrees clockwise from north. The dot is NOT a degraded dart — it is the correct mark for “here, facing unknown”, and a port that defaulted a missing heading to 0 would draw a north-pointing arrow at a rider standing at a kerb, who would act on it.

**Non-finite readings are spelled `"NaN"` and `"Infinity"` as STRINGS**, because JSON has neither. A suite must decode them to its own language's non-finite values before calling — the rows that use them exist to pin that a non-finite reading is treated as *no reading*, so a port that passed the string straight through would be testing string handling and reporting a pass.

cases.name: an-ordinary-gps-fix-draws-its-circle
cases.why: A phone with a clear sky reports 10–30 m. The everyday case, and what the circle is for: the difference between "you are here" and "you are somewhere in here".

cases.name: no-accuracy-reported-draws-nothing
cases.why: A platform that gives a position and no confidence in it. Inventing a radius would be inventing the uncertainty as well as the position.

cases.name: a-desktop-ip-fix-is-too-coarse-to-draw
cases.why: A desktop browser geolocating by IP routinely answers tens of kilometres. A 15 km circle measures nothing a rider can use — it is a picture of the app being confused, and the honest output is the mark alone.

cases.name: a-circle-smaller-than-the-mark-is-not-drawn
cases.why: A 3 m radius is smaller than the dot painted over it, so it reads as a rendering artefact rather than as precision. Nothing useful to show either.

cases.name: exactly-at-the-floor-is-drawn
cases.why: Inclusive boundary. An off-by-one written as `>` rather than `>=` shows up only here, and 8 m is a plausible real reading from a good fix.

cases.name: exactly-at-the-ceiling-is-drawn
cases.why: The other inclusive boundary, pinned separately because the two comparisons are written independently and only one is usually tested.

cases.name: a-non-finite-accuracy-draws-nothing
cases.why: The same guard as the heading rule: a non-finite reading is an absence, and a circle of undefined radius is a shape no engine agrees about.

accuracyRadiusM.doc:
The radius to draw around a fix, in metres, or absent where a circle would say less than nothing. Exact equality; `null` is the language's absent value. A circle is a claim about uncertainty and a wrong one is worse than none — the thresholds are 8 m (below which the circle is smaller than the mark on top of it) and 2 000 m (above which it covers the screen and says only that the app is confused).
